implementation_notes: The standard library supplies the pieces, not the policy: classify the failure (a typed exception, std::error_code, or the return value), test the attempt budget, and wait with std::this_thread::sleep_for(<chrono>) before the next attempt - sleep_for blocks for at least the requested duration, so the delay is a floor rather than a promise. Keep the loop interruptible by checking a std::stop_token (C++20) or an atomic flag between attempts, and prefer returning the classified error over the last exception so the caller sees why the attempts stopped. The classic structure stays justified here: no standard facility composes retry policies, so hand-rolling the loop around a documented policy object is the norm.
pitfalls: sleep_for is a floor, not an exact delay, and it is not interruptible: a long final delay keeps shutdown waiting unless the loop checks a stop_token between attempts.
Catching everything loses the classification - retry on std::system_error or timeout categories only, never on std::logic_error.
A loop that swallows the exception and returns a default value turns a transient failure into silent data loss; rethrow or return the classified error.
A std::async/std::future used as the retried operation leaves the failed future's exception unobserved unless the loop gets or discards it explicitly.

variants.name: Error-code loop over std::expected, no exceptions (C++23)
variants.idiom_name: std::expected<T, Error> retry driver with monadic or_else/transform_error
variants.implementation_notes: In codebases built with exceptions disabled (embedded, some game and trading toolchains) the retry driver is a plain loop over std::expected: the operation returns std::expected<T, Error>, the classifier inspects the error value instead of an exception type, and the loop re-invokes until success, budget exhaustion or a permanent error - std::unexpected carries the reason. The monadic surface (and_then, or_else, transform_error) lets the same wrapper be expressed as a function from a callable returning expected to the same type, which is why this form reads as functional error propagation rather than exception control flow. Choose it when the toolchain is C++23 and the API contract is no-throw; the exception-based loop stays simpler where exceptions are allowed.
pitfalls: std::expected is C++23-only: feature-test __cpp_lib_expected, and pre-C++23 code needs a polyfill (for example tl::expected) whose monadic helpers must be checked before relying on and_then/or_else.
An error type that cannot distinguish transient from permanent (a plain enum with one 'failed' value) makes classification impossible - design the error type with the retry decision in mind.
Monadic chains hide attempt bookkeeping; keep the retry driver an explicit loop so attempts and delays stay observable.
value() on an unexpected expected throws bad_expected_access, which is a terminate in a no-exceptions build: read error() instead.
